extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of philosophy and Bacon studies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used in a scholarly introduction to evaluate Francis Bacon's authorship, philosophical doctrines, moral and psychological views, scientific attainments, and historical significance. Useful for judging Bacon's merits and defects as philosopher, reformer, and man of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship evidence for Latin works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use documentary and palaeographic evidence (letters, negotiations about translations) and internal manuscript signs (corrections in Bacon's own hand, style similarity) to attribute Latin works to Bacon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Tenison's evidence and proximity to translation negotiations; MS of Cogitata et Visa corrected throughout in Bacon's handwriting; Commentarius Solutus entries made almost indifferently in English and Latin; Latin of Novum Organum bears the same mark of genius as Bacon's English. Use handwriting corrections, bilingual manuscript practice, stylistic affinity, and contemporary accounts as corroborating indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: Founder of a philosophical school
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether an author 'founded' a school by checking explicit repudiation of sectarian founding and the degree to which his method and expressions shaped later empirical traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes Bacon 'was not the founder of a philosophical school' (he repudiated such a character) but his exposition of method contributed to the empirical school of English philosophy. Evaluate both explicit statements by the author and downstream influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical focus vs metaphysical speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the author's attitude to ontological/metaphysical questions by whether he treats such questions with 'disinterested, if not a contemptuous, silence' and avoids speculative metaphysics in favour of practical enquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon assumed ordinary distinction of mind and matter and avoided deep metaphysical elaboration. When evaluating, check whether the writer treats metaphysical topics as outside human knowledge or central to enquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological doctrine: duality of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and evaluate claims about human psychology such as the twofold division of soul into a divine rational soul and an irrational (sensible/produced) soul derived from the elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the author grounds the doctrine (citations to De Augmentis), how he reconciles it with theology, and its later influence or disappearance among successors. Note whether the 'irrational' soul is treated as corporeal ('planoa substantia corporea').

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mental faculties and their relation to learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the author's taxonomy—Intellectus (including Memory, Imagination, Reason) and the mapping of History->Memory, Poetry->Imagination, Philosophy->Reason—to evaluate his theory of mind and educational divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check how the author treats Logic and Ethic as arts using faculties, the roles assigned to Imagination, and whether 'Intellectus' is used as a generic term. Use these mappings when judging coherence of his psychology and program for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Perception and Sense (reflex vs conscious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the presence and use of a distinction roughly between unconscious/reflex actions and conscious affections (e.g., magnet attraction or digestion vs conscious perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights this as Bacon's useful distinction. When assessing psychological claims, see whether reflexive processes are separated from conscious ones and whether examples are given (magnet, union of bubbles, digestion, heartbeat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological sources of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the author's account of the sources of knowledge: experience as the ordinary source, with reserved roles for Divine Inspiration and an inner 'lumen' or conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage lists (1) sense/induction/reason, (2) divine inspiration (scriptural), and (3) an 'internal' light akin to conscience. Use this tripartite scheme to evaluate claims about epistemic foundation and limits of human knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy of inductive treatment in Logic, Ethics, Politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the author explicitly recommends inductive methods for traditionally non-empirical disciplines (Logic, Ethics, Politics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states Bacon conceived that Logic, Ethics, and Politics ought to be treated inductively. When evaluating his methodological program, test for concrete proposals or implementations of inductive procedures in these fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to theory of memory, association, and 'idola'
rubrics_metrics.description: Value the presence and substance of contributions such as theory of memory and association (Novum Organum ii.26) and aphorisms on Idola Tribus and Idola Specus as indicators of original insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specific references to Novum Organum and the 'idola' aphorisms to assess originality and influence on later psychology and epistemology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral philosophy: roots and classification of good
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate moral theory by whether it searches for 'the roots of good and evil' (deep, not prolix inquiry), distinguishes private (individual) and public (common) good, and locates morality in relation to theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises searching for roots of moral concepts and notes Bacon's division into Bonum Individuale (private) and Bonum Communum (public), and the subordination of ethics to theology. Use depth of analysis, grounding of moral concepts, and stance toward theology as assessment axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral philosophy: subordination to theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether ethical inquiry is treated as 'hand-maid' to theology—useful within limits but ultimately subordinate and required to serve theological ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author quotes Bacon's explicit statement that Moral Philosophy should 'in famulitium theologiae recipi' and play an obsequious role. Evaluate how this affects the autonomy and aims of ethics in the author's system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific attainments: three main charges
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging scientific competence, consider the three charges: (1) he was a dilettante in science; (2) imperfect acquaintance with existing knowledge; (3) grossly exaggerated the defects of his own time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three evaluative points as a checklist when assessing Bacon's scientific standing. Corroborate with examples of omissions and errors noted in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical and technical familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the author was conversant with contemporary mathematical and technical advances (Napier's logarithms, Kepler, Archimedes, methods for specific gravity, theory of equilibrium, theory of accelerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text lists numerous omissions (no mention of Napier's Logarithms, Galilean results on acceleration, Archimedes/Apollonius/Stevinus, methods for specific gravity). Use presence or absence of awareness of these landmarks as a metric of scientific thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method and attention to differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess experimental competence by whether experiments control obvious variables, include decisive variations, and whether the investigator displays the faculty of distinguishing subtle differences ('contemplationes, et morari et haerere in omni subtilitate differentiarum').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author faults Bacon for overlooking an obvious circumstance in a windmill experiment and for lacking the faculty of patiently studying particular facts. Use checks for experimental design rigor and analytic attention to differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit as reformer vs merit as theorist
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the author's value as proponent of a new method and organizer of enquiry (a 'logician' and reformer) versus his shortcomings as a systematic philosopher or as a detailed scientist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concluding assessment: Bacon's merit lies chiefly in 'assertion of the necessity of a new method, of a new range of studies, of a new spirit of enquiry.' When evaluating his legacy, weigh methodological influence separately from doctrinal precision or technical mastery.
